title: Reading the Meeting Room
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership field note argues that leading a meeting well starts with diagnosis rather than action: before deciding how to intervene, a leader must read what the meeting and its people actually need. Drawing on research into sense-making and situational awareness, it warns that leaders routinely misread situations through the lens of their own preferences, emotions and expertise, and recommends a recurring self-question about what the room needs from them right now. The key discipline is to read behavior rather than the meeting's stated purpose, illustrated by a deadline-alignment meeting that turns out to be about blame and trust. The piece then names four diagnostic cues: shifts in energy and engagement, deviations from people's normal participation baseline, conspicuous silences about topics that should logically come up, and circular arguments that signal the stated topic is not the real one. It closes by insisting diagnosis only matters if it changes behavior, urging leaders to treat the agenda as a hypothesis rather than a script.
points: Leaders should classify the situation ("What am I looking at?") before generating responses ("What should I do?"), since their own preferences often bias the reading.
A change in group energy, up or down, is itself the signal to do something different, regardless of its direction.
When a normally quiet person pushes hard or a vocal one goes silent, the deviation from baseline matters more than the content of what is said.
Topics, names and questions a group avoids reveal self-censorship around risk, blame and bad news.
Relitigating a settled issue indicates an unaddressed underlying problem, and the group will keep circling until it is named.
quotes: This sounds obvious, but research on sense-making and situational awareness reveals that leaders routinely misread meetings and other situations, particularly when their own preferences, emotions, and expertise become the lens through which they interpret what is happening.
Those adept at reading the meeting recognize patterns and classify the situation before generating alternatives. “What am I looking at?” comes before “What should I do?

A leader who pushes ahead with the coordination agenda misses the real task of working through the issues of blame and trust. A leader who reads the behavior first recognizes that this is a moment of accountability and trust disguised as a scheduling meeting.

When a usually quiet team member suddenly pushes hard on a point, or a usually vocal one goes silent, the content matters less than the fact that the pattern has changed. People deviate from their normal participation baseline for a reason, and that reason is rarely random.

People self-censor around risk, blame, and bad news long before they will say so directly. The gap between what should logically come up and what actually does is often a clue to the leader that they must raise an issue.

The circling is rarely about the specifics of the plan, date, or process being reargued. It is a sign that something underneath, unresolved, or unspoken hasn’t been addressed. The group will keep orbiting it until it is.
Reading the room correctly and then running the original agenda anyway is not leadership. The best leaders treat the agenda and meeting plan as a hypothesis rather than a script.
